Early signal•ClinicalTrials.gov results record•September 8, 2026

Ketogenic diet trial posts inconclusive 12-week cognitive results

Registry results showed small, imprecise within-group ADAS-Cog changes and more nonserious adverse events with the ketogenic diet; no between-group effect estimate was reported.

Key quantitative results: For the primary ADAS-Cog11 outcome, mean change was −0.52 points (95% CI −2.85 to 1.81; n=32) with ketogenic diet and +0.96 (95% CI −1.04 to 2.97; n=37) with the comparator; lower scores are better, and the registry reports no between-group estimate.

ManagementNonpharmacologic care

Added September 8, 2026 · NCT03860792; ClinicalTrials.gov results first posted 2026-09-08

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The registry results are insufficient to recommend a ketogenic diet as an AD cognitive treatment, particularly without a reported between-group estimate.

Study design

Eighty-four adults aged 50–90 with Alzheimer disease and CDR 0.5 or 1 were randomized 1:1 to a 12-week ketogenic diet or Therapeutic Lifestyle Changes diet; outcome assessors were masked.

Key quantitative results

  • For the primary ADAS-Cog11 outcome, mean change was −0.52 points (95% CI −2.85 to 1.81; n=32) with ketogenic diet and +0.96 (95% CI −1.04 to 2.97; n=37) with the comparator; lower scores are better, and the registry reports no between-group estimate.
  • Completion was 32/42 versus 38/42. Nonserious adverse events affected 17/42 versus 9/42, including diarrhea in 9/42 versus 0/42; no serious events or deaths were reported in either group.

What changed

Primary results were first posted to ClinicalTrials.gov on September 8, 2026.

Strength of evidence

Randomized evidence, but small, short, incompletely analyzed and currently registry-only, with no reported between-group treatment effect.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The posted results do not establish cognitive benefit from a ketogenic diet in mild AD and identify a meaningful tolerability burden.

Field medical relevance

Supports careful counseling about uncertain cognitive benefit, adherence demands and gastrointestinal effects when patients ask about ketogenic diets.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, formal guideline endorsement, commercial availability or coverage change is established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Do these results prove that ketogenic diets have no benefit?
No. The 12-week trial is small and the registry does not report a between-group estimate, so the result is inconclusive rather than definitive.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Fourteen randomized participants did not complete the study, with more withdrawals in the ketogenic group.
  • The registry reports arm-specific change estimates but no adjusted between-group comparison, and no peer-reviewed primary results publication was identified.

Primary source · Structured registry record

University of Kansas Medical Center. Therapeutic Diets in Alzheimer's Disease (TDAD). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03860792. Results first posted September 8, 2026.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed systematic review and meta-analysis•September 7, 2026

Cannabinoid meta-analysis finds no behavioral or cognitive benefit in dementia

Nine small randomized trials did not show improved agitation, neuropsychiatric symptoms or cognition, while somnolence was more frequent with cannabinoids.

Key quantitative results: Cannabinoids did not improve CMAI agitation (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.71 to 0.55; I²=84%) or NPI-NH total symptoms (SMD −0.02, 95% CI −1.00 to 0.96; I²=67%).

ManagementNeuropsychiatric symptom management

Added September 8, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s10072-026-09347-z; PMID:42704497

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The pooled estimates do not support cannabinoids for dementia-related agitation or cognition, and the increased somnolence signal matters in frail populations.

Study design

Nine randomized controlled trials with 334 participants who had Alzheimer disease or dementia; databases were searched through November 2025 and outcomes were synthesized with random-effects models.

Key quantitative results

  • Cannabinoids did not improve CMAI agitation (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −1.71 to 0.55; I²=84%) or NPI-NH total symptoms (SMD −0.02, 95% CI −1.00 to 0.96; I²=67%).
  • MMSE results were also inconclusive (SMD 0.86, 95% CI −16.33 to 18.06; I²=96%). Overall adverse events were similar, but somnolence was more frequent (RR 2.03, 95% CI 1.29–3.20).

What changed

A September synthesis combines nine randomized trials and quantifies both the absence of pooled symptom benefit and the somnolence risk.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-certainty evidence for behavioral outcomes and low-certainty evidence for cognition; estimates are limited by small trials and substantial heterogeneity.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Current evidence does not support cannabinoids to improve agitation, neuropsychiatric symptoms or cognition in dementia.

Field medical relevance

Useful for evidence-based discussions about off-label cannabinoid use and for separating anecdotal response from controlled evidence.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, guideline endorsement or coverage change follows from this evidence synthesis.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a clinical practice guideline?
No. It is a systematic review and meta-analysis, with no new recommendation, authorization or coverage decision.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Only 334 participants were included across nine trials, and formulations, doses and populations varied.
  • Heterogeneity was high for CMAI, NPI-NH total and MMSE outcomes, limiting precision and generalizability.

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Tudella GCN, Klostermann AU, Menegucci G, et al. Efficacy and safety of cannabinoid-based interventions for behavioral and cognitive symptoms in dementia: systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurol Sci. Published September 7, 2026. doi:10.1007/s10072-026-09347-z.

Field-changing•FDA 510(k) decision and official company announcement•August 19, 2026

FDA cleared the PrecivityAD2 mass-spectrometry blood test

The cleared test combines Aβ42/Aβ40 and p-tau217/np-tau217 into an Amyloid Probability Score 2 for symptomatic adults aged 40 or older; current LDT availability and rollout of the cleared IVD remain distinct.

Key quantitative results: FDA 510(k) K253240 decision date: August 19, 2026.

BiomarkersBloodAβ42Aβ40Biological confirmation

Added September 4, 2026 · FDA 510(k) K253240

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

FDA clearance adds a mass-spectrometry approach with dual cutoffs to the authorized blood-test landscape. The intended population begins at age 40 and requires symptoms plus experienced clinical assessment. C2N states that the cleared product rollout is forthcoming; the currently offered PrecivityAD2 LDT is not automatically the same regulatory product.

Study design

Pivotal clinical validation reported by C2N in 1,142 symptomatic participants, using amyloid PET as reference and a dual-cutoff APS2 interpretation.

Key quantitative results

  • FDA 510(k) K253240 decision date: August 19, 2026.
  • Reported clinical validation n=1,142.
  • Reported positive-category PPV 97.6% and negative-category NPV 93.1%.
  • The 'Likely Positive' intermediate category was 17.3% of participants and had PPV 77.3%.

What changed

A laboratory mass-spectrometry algorithm became an FDA-cleared IVD aid for amyloid-pathology assessment.

Strength of evidence

High for regulatory status; detailed subgroup and analytical interpretation should follow the FDA decision summary and final labeling.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The result is an aid, not standalone diagnosis. The intermediate group remains clinically meaningful and prevalence affects predictive value.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions about LDT versus cleared IVD, sample shipping, turnaround, age range, algorithm transparency, and comparison with automated immunoassays.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Adds a centralized mass-spectrometry model to the clinical landscape; comparisons with immunoassays require same-cohort evidence.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Clearance does not establish payer coverage, payment, shipping logistics, or patient cost.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is the FDA-cleared version available today?
C2N states that availability of the cleared test is expected in coming months; the currently available test is described as an LDT. Verify at ordering.
Can it replace PET or CSF?
The clearance is as an aid in assessment, not a standalone diagnosis. Intermediate or discordant results may still require confirmatory evaluation.
Can APS2 be compared directly with an immunoassay concentration?
No. It combines multiple mass-spectrometry ratios in a proprietary score with its own thresholds and intended use.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Company announcement supplied headline PPV/NPV
  • Rollout timing uncertain
  • Predictive values depend on study prevalence
  • Algorithm-specific score is not cross-platform interchangeable

Primary source

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. PrecivityAD2 Test. 510(k) K253240. Decision August 19, 2026.

Field-changing•FDA 510(k) decision summary•August 19, 2026

FDA cleared Elecsys pTau217 Plasma with fixed negative, intermediate, and positive cutoffs

In 958 valid participants aged 55 or older, the automated assay produced PPV 88.5%, NPV 95.3%, and 19.9% intermediate results against amyloid PET, with lower positive predictive value in primary care.

Key quantitative results: Cutoffs: ≤0.223 pg/mL negative; >0.223 to ≤0.378 intermediate; >0.378 positive.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Biological confirmation

Added September 4, 2026 · FDA 510(k) K261686

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The decision summary supplies public cutoffs, subgroup performance, and analytical data for a fully automated single-analyte test. Lower prevalence in primary care reduced PPV, illustrating why the same cutoff does not produce the same post-test probability in every setting.

Study design

Retrospective pivotal analysis of 958 valid symptomatic participants aged 55–85 years; 378 amyloid-PET positive and 580 negative. About 25% were from primary care and 75% from specialty settings.

Key quantitative results

  • Cutoffs: ≤0.223 pg/mL negative; >0.223 to ≤0.378 intermediate; >0.378 positive.
  • Positive category: 285/322 amyloid positive, PPV 88.5% (95% CI, 84.9%–91.4%). Negative category: 424/445 amyloid negative, NPV 95.3% (93.1%–96.8%).
  • 191/958 (19.9%) were intermediate; 72/191 (37.7%) were amyloid positive.
  • Primary-care PPV was 78.3% versus 90.2% in secondary/tertiary care. Measuring range was 0.056–2.40 pg/mL; within-lab CV was about 1.2%–5.0%.

What changed

A high-throughput, single-analyte p-tau217 assay gained a public FDA intended use and fixed three-zone interpretation across primary and specialty settings.

Strength of evidence

High regulatory and clinical-validity evidence with public analytical and subgroup data; prospective clinical utility is not established.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The test may aid amyloid-pathology assessment but cannot be used alone. Intermediate results and positive results near the cutoff may require PET or CSF depending on context.

Field medical relevance

The decision summary provides concrete answers on prevalence, predictive value, cutoffs, sample handling, and primary-care generalizability.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Important automated-laboratory comparator for ultrasensitive platforms; performance claims must remain within the same intended use and reference.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Roche and Quest announced future rollout, but clearance alone does not establish current local availability, coverage, or payment.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can this replace PET or CSF?
Not universally. The label says it is an aid and not standalone; intermediate and some positive results require clinical follow-up.
Why is PPV lower in primary care?
Amyloid prevalence was lower. Predictive value changes with pretest probability even when assay sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.
Can it be used to monitor treatment?
No monitoring or prediction claim is established in the cleared intended use.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective archived-sample design
  • Predominantly White US cohort
  • Subgroup confidence intervals widen for underrepresented groups
  • Clinical utility and serial monitoring not tested

Primary source

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Elecsys Phospho-Tau (217P) Plasma. 510(k) K261686. Decision August 19, 2026.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed prospective implementation study•August 13, 2026

A prospective memory-clinic study found modest diagnostic changes but higher confidence after BBM disclosure

In 450 specialty-clinic patients, a p-tau181/GFAP/NfL panel changed the suspected etiology in 5% and raised median diagnostic confidence from 80% to 90%; intermediate results were common.

Key quantitative results: N=450; 149 SCD, 67 MCI, 162 dementia, and other syndromes.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau181GFAPDifferential diagnosis

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.28864

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This study measured actual diagnostic workflow impact, not just AUC. The panel most often changed confidence rather than the diagnosis. Because it used p-tau181 and academic specialty clinics, it should not be assumed to predict the impact of current p-tau217 workflows or primary care.

Study design

Consecutive prospective cohort at three Dutch academic memory clinics; blood results were presented after standard workup during multidisciplinary meetings, with later CSF/PET disclosure when available.

Key quantitative results

  • N=450; 149 SCD, 67 MCI, 162 dementia, and other syndromes.
  • Median diagnostic confidence rose from 80% (IQR 70%–90%) to 90% (70%–90%); P<0.001.
  • Etiologic diagnosis changed in 23 patients (5%); syndrome diagnosis changed in 6 (1%).
  • Among 356 evaluated for AD probability, 42% were high, 28% intermediate, and 30% low. In the CSF/PET subset, intermediate results occurred in 24%–39% depending on the model.

What changed

The field gained prospective evidence about how a multimarker panel altered real multidisciplinary decisions and confidence.

Strength of evidence

Moderate implementation evidence; no randomized comparator, incomplete reference testing, and an older p-tau marker constrain causal conclusions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Biomarkers may refine confidence even when they rarely change diagnosis. A high intermediate rate can blunt practical value and create downstream testing.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to questions from memory clinics and health systems about where in the workflow to reveal results and what outcome to measure.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Direct example of Simoa multianalyte use in a diagnostic workflow; does not establish an authorized panel or a commercial superiority claim.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No reimbursement or economic endpoint; intermediate classifications may add confirmatory testing.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did the panel improve diagnostic accuracy?
The main result was change in diagnosis and confidence, not a randomized improvement in patient outcomes. Reference testing was available in only 52%.
Will p-tau217 have the same impact?
Unknown. The authors note that p-tau217 may reduce intermediate results, but that workflow requires prospective testing.
Is this primary-care evidence?
No. It was conducted in academic specialty memory clinics.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • No randomization
  • Only 52% had CSF or amyloid PET
  • Academic specialty setting
  • p-tau181 rather than p-tau217
  • Quanterix employee coauthor and disclosed relationships

Primary source · DOI

Vigneswaran S, Verberk IMW, Boonkamp L, et al. Plasma Alzheimer biomarkers and diagnostic decision-making in memory clinics. JAMA Netw Open. 2026;9:e2628864. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.28864.

Field-changing•FDA approval and official sponsor release•August 13, 2026

FDA approved Tauklarify as a second tau PET tracer for cognitively impaired adults

Florquinitau F 18 (formerly MK-6240) is now approved to identify tau neurofibrillary tangle pathology in adults with cognitive impairment being evaluated for AD, with label cautions against standalone exclusion or confirmation.

Key quantitative results: Study 1 (n=279): reader positive percent agreement 80%–88% and negative percent agreement 98%–99%.

BiomarkersTau PETTau tanglesDisease staging

Added September 4, 2026 · FDA approval:Tauklarify:2026-08-13

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The United States now has a second approved tau PET tracer. Its pivotal reader studies used a prespecified reference based on cognitive status and amyloid PET—not universal autopsy. A negative scan does not exclude tau pathology, especially earlier disease, and use in non-AD tauopathies is not established.

Study design

Two blinded image-reader studies with five readers per study and 617 total participants: 152 mild AD dementia, 157 MCI, and 308 cognitively unimpaired.

Key quantitative results

  • Study 1 (n=279): reader positive percent agreement 80%–88% and negative percent agreement 98%–99%.
  • Study 2 (n=338): positive percent agreement 68%–82% and negative percent agreement 93%–99%.
  • Generalized Fleiss κ was 0.92 and 0.86 in the two studies.
  • Safety exposure included 1,734 participants; headache was reported in 0.7%.

What changed

MK-6240 moved from research use to an FDA-approved radiodiagnostic intended for cognitively impaired adults under AD evaluation.

Strength of evidence

High for authorization and reader reproducibility; reference-standard and early-stage sensitivity limitations remain material.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Tau PET choice may now expand beyond flortaucipir, but ordering, reading, distribution, and payer pathways need implementation.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions about differences from Tauvid, early tau detection, staging, and whether tau PET is required for anti-amyloid therapy. Keep label claims separate from research comparisons.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Changes the PET reference landscape used for blood- and CSF-biomarker studies.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Approval does not establish local tracer supply, PET capacity, payer coverage, or patient cost.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can a negative Tauklarify scan rule out AD tau?
No. The label cautions that performance may be lower earlier in the pathological spectrum and a negative scan does not necessarily exclude tau pathology.
Is it approved for PSP, CTE, or other tauopathies?
No. Safety and effectiveness for non-AD tauopathies have not been established.
Is it proven superior to Tauvid?
The separate HEAD study found direct comparative differences, but the FDA approval itself does not create a universal superiority claim across all uses.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Reference combined cognition and amyloid PET rather than universal autopsy
  • Positive agreement varied by study/reader
  • Early pathology can be missed
  • Real-world availability and coverage not established in the approval

Primary source

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Tauklarify (florquinitau F 18) novel drug approval. Approved August 13, 2026.

GuidelinesManagementRisk reduction

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is guidance for normal cognition and MCI, not evidence that established AD dementia can be reversed.

Evidence basis and population

WHO evidence synthesis for adults without dementia, with a life-course and public-health focus.

Key recommendations

  • Recommendations include physical activity, cardiometabolic care, social engagement, and reducing air-pollution exposure.

Does the 45% estimate describe an individual treatment effect?
No. WHO cites population-level modifiable risk, not a trial-proven 45% benefit for a person.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed pooled longitudinal cohort study•July 14, 2026

Pooled cohorts linked very high p-tau217 to 38% five-year progression risk in unimpaired adults

Among 2,684 selected cognitively unimpaired participants, very high p-tau217 was associated with 38% five-year absolute risk of cognitive impairment, but the authors cautioned against individual prognosis in unselected populations.

Key quantitative results: 478 participants progressed to cognitive impairment.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Prognosis

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jama.2026.12556

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study provides absolute rather than only relative risk, which is useful for prevention-trial planning. It does not justify routine testing of asymptomatic people: cohorts were selected, assay values were standardized within study, and longer-horizon estimates were sparse.

Study design

Harmonized analysis of 2,684 cognitively unimpaired participants across six North American, Japanese, and Australian cohorts; median follow-up 5.4 years and maximum 13.5 years.

Key quantitative results

  • 478 participants progressed to cognitive impairment.
  • Per 1-SD higher baseline p-tau217, HR 1.38 (95% CI, 1.30–1.46); adjusted for amyloid PET Centiloids, HR 1.32 (1.24–1.41).
  • Five-year absolute risk was 24% (95% CI, 20%–28%) for high and 38% (33%–43%) for very high p-tau217.
  • Very-high group annualized PACC change was −0.07 units/year versus +0.03 in the low group.

What changed

The report translated p-tau217 into time-specific absolute progression risk across multiple cohorts.

Strength of evidence

Moderate prognostic evidence with multicohort consistency; clinical utility and calibration in unselected care populations remain unknown.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Most people in the very-high group did not progress within five years. A high result is not a diagnosis or a deterministic forecast.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions from clinicians and researchers about screening, counseling, and prevention-trial enrollment. Keep research prognosis separate from approved diagnostic intended use.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Cross-assay harmonization by SD does not make concentrations or cutoffs interchangeable across platforms.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No evidence supports payer coverage for asymptomatic prognostic testing; downstream counseling and confirmatory testing could be substantial.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should asymptomatic adults get p-tau217 testing?
Not on this evidence. The study calls for validation in unselected populations and does not establish a care pathway or benefit from disclosure.
Does 38% mean a person has a 38% personal risk?
It is a group estimate in selected cohorts, not a fully calibrated individual prediction.
Does p-tau217 add beyond amyloid PET?
The association persisted after Centiloid adjustment, but incremental decision value and utility were not tested.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Selected research and trial cohorts
  • Within-cohort standardization limits universal thresholds
  • Sparse 10-year data
  • Outcome definitions varied by cohort
  • No disclosure-impact trial

Primary source · DOI

Buckley RF, Townsend DL, Birkenbihl CJ, et al. Prognostic value of blood-based p-tau217 levels for progression to cognitive impairment. JAMA. Published online July 14, 2026. doi:10.1001/jama.2026.12556.

CELIA randomized 416 anti-amyloid-naive participants with MCI or mild AD dementia to intrathecal diranersen or placebo for 18 months.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed individual-participant-data meta-analysis•July 13, 2026

A 49,227-person meta-analysis defined an 11–26 Centiloid caution zone for amyloid PET

Across 53 studies, values below 11 Centiloids were high-confidence negative and values above 26 high-confidence positive in a data-driven model; the 11–26 range warrants contextual interpretation rather than an automatic binary call.

Key quantitative results: Data-driven single positivity cutoff: 18 Centiloids (95% CI, 16–19; I²=97%).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidCentiloidBiological confirmation

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1001/jama.2026.13116

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This large analysis gives a defensible framework for talking about borderline amyloid PET quantitation. It does not replace expert visual interpretation and showed substantial between-study heterogeneity. A blood, CSF, or repeat imaging result may be useful when quantitation and visual read disagree.

Study design

Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of 49,227 scans from 53 studies and five tracers in 15 countries. Gaussian mixture and visual-read correspondence methods were analyzed separately.

Key quantitative results

  • Data-driven single positivity cutoff: 18 Centiloids (95% CI, 16–19; I²=97%).
  • Double cutoff: <11 high-confidence negative (95% CI, 9–13) and >26 high-confidence positive (24–28); I²=95% for both.
  • Visual-read correspondence in 35,045 scans produced a 27-Centiloid cutoff (95% CI, 24–30) and κ=0.86 (0.83–0.89).
  • The intermediate range was 11–26 Centiloids.

What changed

The field gained pooled quantitative benchmarks and an explicit indeterminate interval rather than another single-study threshold.

Strength of evidence

Strong quantitative synthesis with high heterogeneity and no single harmonized visual-read protocol.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Borderline Centiloid values should be treated as uncertainty, especially when used for diagnosis or treatment eligibility.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to interpreting blood–PET discordance and to explaining why a binary threshold may not reflect the uncertainty near the decision boundary.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Defines uncertainty in a common reference used for blood-assay validation; discordance may reflect PET threshold choice rather than blood-assay error alone.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Clarifying intermediate scans may require additional testing; no cost analysis was performed.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can 18 Centiloids be used as the universal positive cutoff?
No. It is a meta-estimate with high heterogeneity; method, tracer, visual read, and intended use matter.
Should quantitation override the visual read?
No. The authors state that expert visual assessment remains crucial.
What should happen in the 11–26 range?
Review scan quality and visual interpretation and consider another validated biomarker when uncertainty would change management.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • High between-study heterogeneity
  • No harmonized visual-read protocol
  • Limited representation from several world regions
  • Not a randomized clinical utility study

Primary source · DOI

Blazhenets G, Soleimani-Meigooni DN, Chiotis K, et al. Amyloid PET quantitation and Centiloid thresholds in the diagnosis of Alzheimer disease. JAMA. Published online July 13, 2026. doi:10.1001/jama.2026.13116.

Lecanemab labeling adds subcutaneous treatment initiation

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Route convenience changes delivery planning, while amyloid confirmation, early symptomatic eligibility and ARIA precautions remain.

Study design

Label update for initiation in MCI or mild AD dementia, with confirmed amyloid pathology.

Subcutaneous dosing can begin at treatment initiation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Initiation and maintenance strengths must remain distinct.

Field medical relevance

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00417-4

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is the kind of comparison that supports a relative performance statement: both tracers were used in the same participants within 45 days. Detection differences could alter staging and trial eligibility. The study did not use autopsy as a universal truth standard and does not make the tracers interchangeable.

Study design

Prospective, nonrandomized, cross-sectional study at eight North American sites; 775 enrolled and 682 completed paired tau PET, amyloid PET, and cognitive assessment within 45 days.

Key quantitative results

  • AUC for AD-related cognitive impairment was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.89–0.95) for MK-6240 versus 0.86 (0.75–0.91) for flortaucipir; P<0.0001.
  • Neocortical tau positivity in cognitively impaired participants was 28% with MK-6240 versus 16% with flortaucipir.
  • Among Aβ-positive participants, the prevalence ratio was 1.74 (95% CI, 1.32–2.29).
  • Regional positivity was concordant in 87% for medial temporal and 94% for neocortical classifications.

What changed

The largest paired comparison showed that tracer selection is not a neutral technical detail, particularly for earlier and neocortical tau detection.

Strength of evidence

Strong comparative clinical-validity evidence for the studied imaging definitions; clinical-outcome utility and autopsy accuracy were not primary endpoints.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Tau PET reports and trial criteria should identify the tracer and threshold. Results from one tracer should not be assumed equivalent to another.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions about why the same patient might stage differently by tracer and whether newer tau PET can refine anti-amyloid or anti-tau trial selection.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Not a blood-assay study, but it affects the imaging reference standard used to validate blood biomarkers and define discordance.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Tracer distribution, reader training, and PET capacity may determine real-world availability; no payer or cost comparison was tested.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was this a true head-to-head comparison?
Yes. Participants received both tau tracers within 45 days, with the same amyloid and cognitive context.
Does more positive mean more accurate?
Not automatically. Greater detection and discrimination were shown, but the reference framework was not universal autopsy confirmation.
Can studies using the two tracers be pooled directly?
Not without tracer-specific harmonization; their binding and dynamic ranges differ.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Nonrandomized
  • 93% of participants identified as White
  • No universal neuropathology reference
  • Cross-sectional primary comparison
  • Sponsor relationships disclosed

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

p-tau217 largely marked amyloid pathology, but many positive symptomatic patients did not meet the study's definition of established AD as the cause of symptoms. A second, later-changing tau marker improved stratification. This is a clinically relevant concept, not yet a commercial or guideline-endorsed pathway.

Study design

Prospective BioFINDER-2 cohort of 572 symptomatic adults (142 SCD, 259 MCI, 171 dementia), with prespecified biomarker thresholds and external validation in Knight ADRC. Established AD required pathology-specific biomarkers plus a compatible clinical assessment.

Key quantitative results

  • 350 of 572 were %p-tau217 positive; 341 (97%) were amyloid positive, but 199 (57%) had established AD.
  • 194 of 350 were also eMTBR-tau243 positive; accuracy for established AD was 81% (95% CI, 76%–84%), PPV 84% (78%–88%), NPV 77% (68%–82%), and sensitivity 82% (76%–87%).
  • Among %p-tau217-positive patients, eMTBR-tau243 identified high tau-PET load with 87% accuracy, 76% PPV, and 90% NPV.
  • Positive eMTBR-tau243 was associated with faster cognitive decline and tau accumulation.

What changed

The study supplied a two-step biological model that separates amyloid confirmation from evidence that more advanced tau pathology may be contributing to symptoms.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence with prespecified thresholds and external validation; clinical utility remains unproven.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A positive p-tau217 test need not prove that AD is the main cause of symptoms, especially when copathology is plausible. A later-stage tau marker may reduce that ambiguity if validated for clinical use.

Field medical relevance

Directly informs conversations about blood–PET discordance, causality versus copathology, staging, and why one blood marker may not answer every clinical question.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Relevant as an emerging marker opportunity, but no Simoa eMTBR-tau243 clinical assay or cross-platform equivalence was established.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No reimbursement or cost-effectiveness analysis; a two-step pathway could reduce or add downstream testing depending on its final intended use.

No. It showed association and classification performance against tau-PET-derived states, but clinical substitution and treatment decisions were not tested.

p-tau217 is closely linked to amyloid biology and can identify coexisting or earlier AD pathology; symptoms may arise from another disease or a mixed process.

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This is a legitimate same-population comparison: identical samples, both PET modalities, and three platforms. Ella and Lumipulse had higher amyloid-PET AUCs than Simoa in this cohort, while Simoa had the lowest analytical detection range. The result illustrates why analytical sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy are different constructs.

Study design

Cross-sectional study of 113 participants (55 AD-continuum, 36 controls, 22 non-AD disorders), all with amyloid and tau PET. Cutoffs were derived in the study using Youden or two-cutoff methods.

Key quantitative results

  • Amyloid-PET AUC: Simoa 0.909 (95% CI, 0.846–0.973), Ella 0.974 (0.945–1.000), Lumipulse 0.965 (0.926–1.000).
  • Ella vs Simoa P=0.009; Lumipulse vs Simoa P=0.019; Ella vs Lumipulse P=0.294.
  • At derived single cutoffs, sensitivity/specificity were 90.9%/87.9% for Simoa, 92.7%/96.6% for Ella, and 94.6%/94.8% for Lumipulse.
  • Tau-PET AUCs were 0.937, 0.989, and 0.985, respectively.

What changed

A direct comparison quantified platform differences without relying on cross-study AUC comparisons.

Strength of evidence

Moderate for a controlled head-to-head signal; low for general platform selection because the cohort was small and cutoffs were not externally validated.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The data do not establish one universally superior assay. Platform-specific cutoffs, intended use, workflow, and external validation remain decisive.

Field medical relevance

A strong example for explaining why lower LLOQ does not automatically yield better clinical classification and why only same-cohort comparisons support relative claims.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Directly relevant to Simoa, Ella, and Lumipulse; supports precise, bounded comparison rather than broad marketing claims.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No cost, coverage, turnaround-time, or capacity comparison was performed.

  • n=113

  • Study-derived thresholds
  • Limited comorbidity spectrum
  • Not a workflow or utility study

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

ADAPT is useful because it separates cutoff derivation from a PET test set and evaluates two platforms. Study design

Stage 1 multicenter study with a 257-person CSF-referenced derivation cohort and an independent 76-person amyloid-PET validation cohort. Dual cutoffs targeted high sensitivity and specificity.

Key quantitative results

  • CSF-referenced AUC: 0.947 for Lumipulse and 0.940 for ALZpath.
  • Lumipulse cutoffs 0.153 and 0.422 pg/mL yielded 94.7% accuracy among definite derivation results; PET validation accuracy was 90.0%.
  • Lumipulse indeterminate results were 19.4% in derivation and 34.2% in PET validation; PET-validation PPV was 90.6% and NPV 88.9%.
  • ALZpath cutoffs 0.220 and 0.486 pg/mL yielded 93.4% definite-result derivation accuracy and 87.5% PET-validation accuracy; 26.3% were indeterminate in validation.

What changed

The study supplied an independent PET test of CSF-derived cutoffs and quantified the tradeoff between confident classification and the size of the intermediate zone.

Strength of evidence

Moderate: multicenter and independent validation, with small PET sample and wide predictive-value intervals.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Field medical relevance

Helpful for explaining why predictive values and gray-zone frequency move when reference method, cohort, and prevalence change.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Direct Simoa–Lumipulse evidence in one development program; analytical sensitivity should not be equated with clinical accuracy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

A larger indeterminate zone increases downstream PET/CSF use; formal cost-effectiveness was not tested.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Which assay was better?
The study was a same-program comparison, but the small PET set and assay-specific cutoffs do not support a broad superiority claim.
What about kidney disease?
Reduced eGFR was associated with higher concentrations and movement into the intermediate range, reinforcing the need for contextual interpretation.
Are these clinical cutoffs universal?
No. They are assay- and population-specific and need prospective pathway validation.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • PET validation n=76
  • Different reference standards in derivation and validation
  • Cutoffs optimized within the program
  • Limited primary-care evidence
  • Potential renal-function effects

Primary source · DOI

Keshavan A, et al. The Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis and Plasma Phospho-Tau217 (ADAPT) study stage 1: validating clinical cut-points against CSF and amyloid PET. Alzheimers Dement. Published online February 19, 2026. doi:10.1002/alz.71147.

Early signal•Peer-reviewed longitudinal cohort study•February 19, 2026

Longitudinal %p-tau217 models estimated symptom onset within a 3–4 year median error

Research-cohort models linked the estimated age of plasma %p-tau217 positivity to later symptom onset, but they are not validated for individual clinical prognosis or asymptomatic screening.

Key quantitative results: Estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity explained 33.7%–61.2% of variance in age at symptom onset across models.

BiomarkersBlood%p-tau217Prognosis

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1038/s41591-026-04206-y

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Two cohort-specific clock models estimated when %p-tau217 crossed positivity and related that timing to symptom onset. Cross-cohort median absolute error remained about 3–4 years. That is promising for trial design, not a basis for counseling an asymptomatic person to a precise year.

Study design

Longitudinal modeling in two selected research cohorts (n=258 and n=345), using serial plasma %p-tau217 and clinical follow-up.

Key quantitative results

  • Estimated age at %p-tau217 positivity explained 33.7%–61.2% of variance in age at symptom onset across models.
  • Median absolute error for symptom-onset prediction was 3.0–3.7 years.
  • Cross-cohort models retained moderate associations, with median absolute error about 3.0–3.7 years.

What changed

The work shifted p-tau217 discussion from binary pathology detection toward time-to-symptom modeling.

Strength of evidence

Early prognostic evidence: longitudinal and replicated across two cohorts, but model-based, selected, and not prospectively tested for clinical decisions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

No current screening or individual prognostic use is established. The near-term use case is enrichment and stratification in prevention trials.

Field medical relevance

Expect questions about telling an asymptomatic person when symptoms will begin. The evidence does not support that use.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Uses mass-spectrometry %p-tau217 and does not establish interchangeability with immunoassay p-tau217 concentrations.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No coverage or cost-effectiveness evidence; asymptomatic testing can create counseling burdens without an established care pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can one blood draw predict the year symptoms start?
No. The median error was measured in years, the cohorts were selected, and the model lacks prospective clinical-utility validation.
Is this an approved intended use?
No. It is a research prognostic model.
Where could it matter first?
Trial enrichment and modeling of prevention-study timelines are more plausible near-term applications than routine care.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Selected research cohorts
  • Model-estimated conversion dates
  • Limited population diversity
  • No decision-impact trial
  • No authorized prognostic claim

Primary source · DOI

Schindler SE, et al. Predicting onset of symptomatic Alzheimer's disease with longitudinal plasma %p-tau217. Nat Med. Published online February 19, 2026. doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04206-y.

Practice-relevant•FDA recall record•February 5, 2026

FDA classified a recall of four Lumipulse plasma p-tau217 cartridge lots after falsely elevated results

Affected lots could shift results toward indeterminate or positive classifications and reduce specificity, prompting discontinuation, result review, and clinician notification.

Key quantitative results: Four p-tau217 cartridge lots were identified: D4C6028U, D4C6029U, D4C6051U, and D4C6052U.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217p-tau217/Aβ42Biological confirmation

Added September 4, 2026 · FDA recall Z-1302-2026

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The problem was analytical and operational, not a change in disease biology. Laboratories using affected lots were instructed to stop use and review prior results because positive bias could produce more indeterminate or positive calls.

Study design

FDA recall record for a voluntary firm action initiated December 11, 2025 and classified/posting updated in 2026.

Key quantitative results

  • Four p-tau217 cartridge lots were identified: D4C6028U, D4C6029U, D4C6051U, and D4C6052U.
  • FDA listed 1,569 affected p-tau217 units distributed in 13 states; the companion ratio recall listed 23 units.
  • The stated failure mode was falsely elevated p-tau217, with more indeterminate or positive results and lower specificity.

What changed

The public record identified a lot-specific source of unexpected positive bias and formalized retrospective result-review actions.

Strength of evidence

High for the existence and scope of the recall; the record does not quantify patient-level false-positive rates.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Unexpected discordance involving affected lots should be evaluated as a potential analytical issue before assuming biological change.

Field medical relevance

Laboratory leaders may ask about lot traceability, corrected reports, clinician notification, and how to separate analytical bias from true blood–CSF–PET discordance.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Highlights lot control, quality assurance, traceability, and reflex-review requirements for high-throughput biomarker testing.

Access or reimbursement relevance

Potential repeat testing and corrected reports may create operational burden; no payment guidance was provided.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should an affected result be repeated?
The recall record instructs customers to discontinue affected lots and review prior results. The laboratory should follow the manufacturer notice and its corrective-reporting procedure.
Does this invalidate all Lumipulse results?
No. The action names specific lots; it does not establish a platform-wide failure.
How large was the positive bias?
The public recall record describes the direction and clinical effect but does not provide a complete patient-level bias distribution.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Recall database does not provide full root-cause investigation
  • No patient outcome analysis
  • Status may change and requires re-verification

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The announcement moved a publicly available five-analyte LDT toward FDA review. The company reported three independent cohorts totaling more than 1,800 symptomatic participants. The release does not provide a decision summary, full contingency tables, or proof of clearance.

Study design

Manufacturer-reported regulatory package based on three independent cohorts with more than 1,800 symptomatic participants. Public patient-level methods and complete performance tables were not provided in the announcement.

Key quantitative results

A marketed CLIA LDT was publicly reported as entering FDA premarket review as a multi-analyte algorithmic assay.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed diagnostic study•January 21, 2026

Lumipulse plasma p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio reduced indeterminate results in a specialty cohort

In 208 symptomatic specialty-care patients, the automated p-tau217/Aβ42 ratio had an AUC of 0.932 against CSF or amyloid PET and produced fewer indeterminate results than p-tau217 alone, but its cutoffs were derived in the same cohort.

Key quantitative results: AUC 0.932 (95% CI, 0.896–0.967) for p-tau217/Aβ42 versus 0.918 (0.880–0.956) for p-tau217 alone.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42Biological confirmation

Added September 4, 2026 · DOI:10.1093/brain/awag001

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study supports a two-cutoff, three-zone interpretation for an automated plasma ratio in symptomatic specialty care. The ratio retained high agreement with CSF or amyloid PET and reduced the gray zone relative to p-tau217 alone. It does not establish performance in primary care or validate a universally transferable threshold.

Study design

Single-center symptomatic cohort; 208 adults aged 51–88 years, including 7 with subjective cognitive decline, 150 with MCI, 12 with AD dementia, and 39 with other diagnoses. The reference was amyloid PET when available or an approved CSF biomarker profile.

Key quantitative results

  • AUC 0.932 (95% CI, 0.896–0.967) for p-tau217/Aβ42 versus 0.918 (0.880–0.956) for p-tau217 alone.
  • Preferred parametric thresholds were ≤0.00370 negative, 0.00371–0.00737 intermediate, and ≥0.00738 positive.
  • Using the study's nonparametric classification, the ratio yielded 20.2% indeterminate results; p-tau217 alone yielded 35.1%.
  • For ratio-classified positives, PPV was 94.6% (95% CI, 88.0%–97.7%); the indeterminate group was 47.6% amyloid positive.

What changed

A same-sample evaluation supplied implementable dual cutoffs and showed how adding Aβ42 could reduce unresolved classifications on an automated platform.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence: clinically relevant cohort and accepted references, but retrospective, single-center, and internally derived thresholds.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The result supports triage logic rather than replacement of CSF or PET. Intermediate results remain common and require a defined follow-up pathway.

Field medical relevance

Useful when discussing why a ratio may change the indeterminate rate, why cutoffs are platform-specific, and why reference modality can influence agreement.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Shows how high-throughput automated immunoassay combinations may improve triage efficiency; it does not compare workflow, cost, or clinical utility against Simoa in a randomized pathway.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No coverage or patient-cost evidence was evaluated.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can the ratio replace PET or CSF?
Not from this study. It was evaluated against PET or CSF and used a three-zone strategy; intermediate and discordant results still require clinical resolution.
Were the thresholds externally validated?
No. They were derived in this cohort, so transport to other settings and prevalence levels remains uncertain.
Was the ratio clearly superior to p-tau217?
It reduced the indeterminate proportion in the same samples. The close AUCs should not be interpreted as universal assay superiority.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center cohort
  • Small PET subgroup
  • Mixed CSF and PET reference standard
  • Thresholds derived rather than externally prespecified
  • Industry relationships and support were reported

Primary source · DOI

Benina N, et al. Clinical validation of the automated Lumipulse G plasma p-tau217/β-amyloid 1-42 ratio. Brain. Published online January 21, 2026. doi:10.1093/brain/awag001.
